summary: Specifies the Simple Certificate Enrolment Protocol (SCEP), a PKI protocol that uses CMS and PKCS #10 over HTTP so devices can request certificates. It evolved from an enrolment protocol originally sponsored by Cisco and is widely supported in client and certificate authority software. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A device needs a digital ID card. SCEP is a simple way for it to ask an authority for one over the web, with the request and answer sealed in a standard envelope.

questions: how do devices enroll for certificates over http
subtitle: A simple protocol for devices to request and renew certificates over HTTP

tldr.problem: Devices need a way to request X.509 certificates from a certificate authority without requiring complex infrastructure, particularly when deployed in the field without pre-existing credentials.
tldr.mechanism: SCEP uses standard cryptographic message syntax (CMS) and PKCS #10 certificate requests wrapped in HTTP POST or GET requests. A device generates a self-signed certificate or uses an existing one to sign the request, which is encrypted to the CA's public key.
tldr.outcome: Devices can enroll for or renew certificates automatically, with optional manual approval from the CA operator, making it practical to deploy certificate-based authentication across thousands of devices.

today: RFC 8894 is an Informational RFC documenting a widely deployed protocol. SCEP is the standard enrollment mechanism for many device classes and remains the de facto industry standard for simple certificate provisioning in constrained environments.

sections.title: Why Devices Need Certificates
sections.content:
X.509 certificates are the foundation for security protocols like TLS, S/MIME, and IPsec. When a device needs a certificate, it requires a certificate management protocol to request or renew it from a certificate authority.

SCEP—the Simple Certificate Enrolment Protocol—is a PKI protocol that evolved from an enrolment mechanism originally sponsored by Cisco. It is now widely supported in both client and server implementations and is relied upon by numerous industry standards. SCEP makes extensive use of Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and PKCS #10 certificate requests, both well-established standards.
sections.eli5: When a device is born, it needs an official digital ID from an authority. SCEP is how it asks for one.

sections.title: How SCEP Works
sections.content:
SCEP consists of two main entities: a client (the device requesting a certificate) and a certificate authority (CA) that issues it. The client must have the CA's fully qualified domain name or IP address and any identification or authorization information required by the CA.

Before any PKI operation, the client retrieves the CA's certificate. Since no public key has yet been exchanged, this transfer happens in the clear. The client should authenticate the CA certificate by checking its fingerprint against locally configured out-of-band data or a previously stored copy.

To request a certificate, the client creates a PKCS #10 certificate request and sends it to the CA enveloped in CMS (encrypted and signed). If the CA requires approval before issuing a certificate, the device enters polling mode, periodically sending poll messages until the CA operator authorizes or rejects the request. When the CA grants the request, the device receives its certificate.
sections.eli5: The device first gets the authority's ID. Then it creates a request for its own ID, scrambles it, and sends it. The authority checks and either sends the ID back or says it is waiting. The device checks back until it gets its ID.

sections.title: Message Protection and Format
sections.content:
SCEP messages use two layers of CMS to protect confidentiality and integrity. The messageData is first encrypted, then the encrypted content is signed with the sender's public key.

All SCEP messages contain a transactionID (a unique text string for the operation), a messageType (specifying the operation: PKCSReq for initial certificate request, RenewalReq for renewal, CertRep for response, CertPoll for polling, GetCert for certificate retrieval, or GetCRL for CRL retrieval), and a senderNonce (a 16-byte random number to prevent replay attacks). Response messages include a pkiStatus (SUCCESS, FAILURE, or PENDING) and a recipientNonce echoing the request's senderNonce.

If the pkiStatus is FAILURE, the message includes a failInfo code describing the failure (badAlg, badMessageCheck, badRequest, badTime, or badCertId) and optional failInfoText providing human-readable details. The CMS envelope protects the privacy of authorization information (such as a shared secret challengePassword) used to authenticate enrollment requests.
sections.eli5: Messages are wrapped in layers: the data scrambled inside an envelope, then signed with the sender's name. Each message gets a unique ID and a random number to make sure no one replays old messages.

sections.title: Certificate Enrollment and Renewal
sections.content:
A device starts enrollment by creating a PKCS #10 certificate request and sending it to the CA in a PKCSReq message. If the CA requires a shared secret for authorization, the device includes a challengePassword attribute in the request. The challengePassword is ideally a one-time value distributed out-of-band to limit reuse.

If the CA can issue the certificate immediately (automatic mode), it responds with a CertRep message with pkiStatus set to SUCCESS, containing the issued certificate. If manual approval is required, the CA responds with pkiStatus set to PENDING. The device then enters polling mode, periodically sending CertPoll messages until the CA either grants the request (SUCCESS) or rejects it (FAILURE).

For certificate renewal, the device uses a RenewalReq message signed with its existing certificate instead of a self-signed one. The CA may optionally verify an additional challengePassword or rely on the signature from the existing certificate for authorization.
sections.eli5: The device asks for a certificate with a secret (challengePassword). Either the authority says yes right away, or it says it is waiting. If waiting, the device keeps asking until it gets an answer.

sections.title: Getting Certificates and CRLs
sections.content:
Beyond enrollment, SCEP supports certificate access and CRL (Certificate Revocation List) queries. A device can retrieve a copy of its own certificate from the CA using a GetCert message (useful for devices that do not store certificates locally), sending the certificate's issuer name and serial number. The CA responds with a CertRep message containing the certificate.

For CRL retrieval, SCEP defines a GetCRL message. However, the RFC recommends that CAs provide CRL Distribution Points (CRLDPs) in certificates or support HTTP certificate-store access via AuthorityInfoAccess extensions, and that GetCRL be used only if the CA does not support these mechanisms.

SCEP does not define a method to request certificate revocation; clients must contact the CA using non-SCEP-defined mechanisms to revoke a certificate.
sections.eli5: The device can ask the authority for a copy of its certificate or a list of revoked certificates if needed. But mainly the authority just gives out certificates and updates the list of bad ones.

viz.caption: Automatic enrollment: device requests and CA approves immediately
Manual enrollment: device polls until CA operator approves
